work_order.understanding:
This revision answers the plan reviewer's objection to the previous one and keeps the rest. The objection was that AC-11 put '[lang]' in its PROVABLY NO-MATCH (silent) list while the same criterion's own ground (b) requires reporting any rule that may match the document root and declares font-size. The reviewer is right and I measured it: the root element is <html lang="en"> (src/web/pages.js:60), so '[lang] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' matches it, sets the root font-size to 2.4rem, and the page h1 then computes 53.76px in Chromium — the same breakage ground (b) exists to catch. '[lang]' is moved out of the silent list in AC-11's how_to_verify and out of the 'provable no-match side' case in tests[], and restated as a ground-(b) REPORTED case beside '*', 'html', ':root' and 'html, body', with 53.76px as its browser control. The reason it looked provably-no-match is that the h1 carries no lang attribute — that is a ground-(a) fact (does it reach the h1) being applied to a ground-(b) rule (does it reach the root), and the two must not be confused. The correction is made in one pass across both places so the criterion, the case list and the guard's contract agree.

A second error the reviewer's objection led me to, and it is mine, not the reviewer's. The previous revision's case 'BUG-4 where the attribute is present' asserted that 'h1[data-testid="page title"] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' is REPORTED, with AC-10 repeating it. I rendered it: the browser leaves the h1 at 22.4px. The shipped h1 carries data-testid="page-title" with a hyphen, so a selector naming 'page title' does not match it — the attribute is present with a different value, which is a proof of non-match and therefore silent under the one-directional contract this same order specifies. The previous revision had written a case that would have made the new guard emit a false failure, on a rule that changes nothing. It is re-stated as silent in AC-10 and in tests[]. It is a better BUG-4 case than the one it replaces, not a weaker one: it still requires the quote-aware split to read the value as one compound, and it now also pins the correct verdict, where the old one pinned a wrong one. I found it only because I re-rendered all 36 selector shapes rather than carrying the previous revision's list forward — the previous revision's own risk section says a change to the guard's vocabulary is a change to a guard, and its example list had changed under it without anyone noticing.

What attempt 1 got wrong, plainly: it built the cascade guard as a thing that pattern-matches selector TEXT, and then asserted, in its own work order section 5 and in the comment above mayReachPageTitle, that being generous in the pre-filter could only produce a failure, never a false pass. That guarantee is false, and each of the four bugs is a way it is false. All four reproduce at 97295e8 and I reproduced each myself on a worktree of origin/sdlc/issue-55: clean tree 275 pass / 0 fail; '[data-testid="page-title"] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' gives 275 pass / 0 fail while Chromium renders the h1 at 38.4px (BUG-1); a second '.page-title { font-size: 2.4rem; }' gives 275 pass / 0 fail, also 38.4px (BUG-2); '.page-title h1 { font-size: 2.4rem; }' gives one failure whose message asserts as fact a change that does not happen, the browser unchanged at 22.4px (BUG-3); 'h1[data-x="a b"] { font-size: 2.4rem; }' throws "the cascade guard cannot read the selector 'h1[data-x="a b"]': the token '[data-x="a'" (BUG-4). None of it is a defect in production code: src/web/pages.js:57 and src/web/styles.css:137 are correct as shipped and this change touches neither.

1. BUG-1 is that guarantee inverted. mayReachPageTitle recognises the class only in dot form: the compound must start with a bare h1, or be *, html or body, or contain '.page-title'. '[data-testid="page-title"]' starts with '[', carries no h1 token and contains no dot, so the pre-filter returns false and the branch is never parsed, while the browser matches that selector against the shipped h1 exactly, at (0,1,0), later in the file, and applies it — I measured 38.4px. The enumerating filter asks 'does this selector look like the ones I thought of'; the question has to be 'can this selector match this element'.

2. BUG-3 is the mirror, and it was attempt 1's own specification. Section 5 said a branch reaches the h1 if 'its last compound carries the page-title class, or its last compound is *, html or body', and parseSelector implements exactly that. Deciding from the last compound alone means any '<something> h1' claims to be the page h1, so '.page-title h1', which targets a descendant h1 of the page title, of which there are none, is reported as an override. The real chain is html < body < main#main < h1, which I confirmed against renderPage('/'), and the page title carries the class itself rather than sitting inside one.

3. BUG-4 was attempt 1's own specification too. Section 5 said 'split comma lists into branches first' and the implementation splits on /\s*>\s*|\s+/, with no regard for brackets or quotes, so the space inside h1[data-x="a b"] cuts one compound in two and the guard throws on CSS its own comment lists as supported vocabulary.

4. BUG-2 is a gap attempt 1's plan designed in. The declaration test pins three literals through .exec, which takes the FIRST rule carrying the class, while the cascade test takes the LAST declaration of each property as its winner. Two tests, two different rules, and nothing joining them: a class declared twice with different values satisfies both while the browser renders 38.4px.

So the diagnosis is rewritten. The guard does not fail because CSS is hard to model. It fails because it decides 'is this the page h1' from the spelling of a selector instead of from the element the markup actually renders, and because it never compares the value the browser finally settles on.

One point of substance carried forward from the previous revision, which the reviewer's transcription got backwards and which I re-measured rather than conceded. The reviewer asks that '*' sit on the list of reach-but-lose cases required to stay CLEAN. It cannot. Appending '* { font-size: 2.4rem; }' to the shipped sheet and reading getComputedStyle on the h1 in Chromium gives fontSize 53.76px and lineHeight 67.2px, not the 22.4px a cascade win at (0,1,0) appears to promise. The class rule does win, and still reads 1.4rem — but '*' sets the ROOT element's font-size to 2.4rem, and every rem in the sheet is measured against the root. The same holds for 'html', ':root' and 'html, body' (28px each at 20px), and now, per the correction above, for '[lang]' (53.76px). Writing '*' as CLEAN would be writing a criterion that certifies a 53.76px page title, which is the defect this ticket exists to prevent, so the reporting rule keeps the second ground: a rule that may match the ROOT element and declares font-size or the font shorthand is reported. Conversely 'h1' at (0,0,1), 'body', 'main *', 'main h1' and 'html body main h1' are all silent — measured at 22.4px each. Attempt 1's suite asserts the '*' case today, in a message that reads "the heading is unaffected", and that message is false. The case is re-stated, not deleted.
work_order.root_cause:
Three causes, all inside the guard this file carries. None is in the shipped app.

The first covers BUG-1 and BUG-3, and it is the one that matters. The guard was given a class NAME and asked to recognise it inside selector text. mayReachPageTitle is a whitelist of spellings ('.page-title' with a dot, 'h1' as a whole compound) and parseSelector sets matchesPageTitle from the last compound alone (lastCarriesClass || lastIsH1 || lastIsUniversal), so both halves of the question 'can this selector match the page h1' are answered by string shape rather than by the element. A whitelist under-approximates: any spelling it did not think of is a false pass (BUG-1, and '[data-testid="page-title"]' is the spelling .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md steers a developer towards). A last-compound test over-approximates: any branch ending in h1 claims to be the page h1 (BUG-3). One decision, made twice, wrong in opposite directions. Attempt 1's claim that being generous in the pre-filter 'can only produce a failure or a throw, never a false pass' is what the implementation violated, and it is false for the same reason: the text filter is not generous with spellings it never imagined.

The second is BUG-4, and it is a direct consequence of the first. The compound splitter is a plain whitespace regex with no bracket or quote awareness, because the guard reasons about selector text as a string: the space inside h1[data-x="a b"] cuts a selector in half and the guard throws on vocabulary its own comment claims to support. Quoting is a property of the text; bracket depth is a property of the text; neither is a property of the element, so a matcher that has to look at elements has to be the thing that tokenises, correctly.

The third is BUG-2, the root font-size, and it is separate from the matcher. The guard compares which declaration wins the cascade; it never compares the value the browser ends up applying. Two consequences, both measured in Chromium on the shipped tree. First, the class rule's winning declaration is never compared with the declaration the page title depends on: the declaration test reads the first rule carrying the class with .exec while the cascade test takes the last declaration of the property as its winner, so a stylesheet declaring .page-title twice with different values satisfies both and renders at 38.4px (BUG-2). Second, even the winning declaration is not resolved: it is written in rem, and a font-size on the root element — '*', 'html', ':root', 'html, body' or any attribute selector naming an attribute the root carries, '[lang]' — changes what every rem in the sheet means, so '* { font-size: 2.4rem; }' loses the cascade at (0,0,0) and still renders the page title at 53.76px. A guard that reads the winning declaration but never the resolved value cannot see either, and the false classification that hid this — treating an attribute selector as a provable no-match because the h1 does not carry that attribute — is the same shape as BUG-1's false pass, made in the opposite direction.
work_order.approach:
Test-only, confined to test/web/pages.test.js, and a rewrite of the matching layer rather than an extension of it. The production files are correct and are not touched. Sections 1 to 4, 6 and 7 are unchanged from the previous revision; section 5 gains the value cross-check and section 8 is new.

The principle: the guard must stop asking 'does this selector look like the page h1' and start asking 'can this selector match the page h1', with the h1 resolved once from the rendered markup — and then it must ask a second question it has never asked, 'what value does the browser end up with'. The first question has exactly one safe answer in each direction — a PROOF of non-match is allowed, nothing else is. The second is a comparison, not a filter, and it is what closes the two holes QA could not see.

1 — Resolve the page h1 into an element, once. Add a helper that scans the rendered HTML's tags, maintains an open-element stack (skipping comments and void elements: area base br col embed hr img input link meta source track wbr), and returns the element carrying data-testid="page-title" together with its ancestor chain, root-first. Each element is { tag, attrs, classes } with attrs a lowercased name -> value map. This is the hook .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md already calls stable, so the guard's notion of the page h1 stops depending on the styling class. I verified the chain against the real renderPage('/') output: html < body < main#main < h1.page-title[data-testid=page-title], with no wrapper between body and main. pageTitleClass() stays and is now read off the returned element, so the two ends of the class-to-rule link keep moving together under a coordinated rename.

2 — One quote- and bracket-aware splitter. Replace both uses of /\s*>\s*|\s+/ with a scanner that walks the branch character by character, tracking a bracket/paren depth and a quote state, and only breaks on whitespace, '>', '+' or '~' at depth 0 outside quotes. Both the matcher and the specificity function must use this one splitter, or they can drift on the same selector. This is what closes BUG-4: 'h1[data-x="a b"]' is one compound, and because the shipped h1 carries no data-x the rule is then provably unable to match it. My prototype of exactly this splitter needed one correction before it was right — 'main > h1' has a space either side of the '>', and a naive scan emits an empty compound between them and then fails to match; the implementer should expect that and handle it, because it is silent rather than loud. Note also that the shipped stylesheet contains a comma list broken across a newline ('.approval-list,\n.experiment-list'), so a newline must count as the whitespace it is.

3 — Match a compound against an element, and the branch against the chain. compoundMatches(compound, element) walks the simple selectors with #id, .class, [attr] (with = ~= ^= $= *= |=), type and * forms, returning false on a proof, true on a match, and undecided otherwise. matchCompounds then requires the rightmost compound to match the target element and each compound to its left to match an element to the left of the one it qualifies — a descendant anywhere in the chain, the element immediately before it for '>'. This is what closes BUG-3: '.page-title h1' needs an ancestor carrying .page-title, and the chain is html < body < main#main < h1, so the rule is provably a no-op and the guard stays quiet. The attribute comparison must be a real value comparison, not a presence test: 'h1[data-testid="page title"]' names a value the h1 does not carry, and that is a proof of non-match, so it is silent (measured: the browser leaves the h1 at 22.4px).

4 — Make the reachability answer one-directional, and delete mayReachPageTitle. branchReaches(branch, chain, target) returns false ONLY on a proof of non-match, and true in every other case, including every case the vocabulary cannot decide. It takes the chain element the rightmost compound must match, so the same primitive answers both questions below.
  - a pseudo-class is undecidable from markup, so strip it and decide on the base. Because :not(), :is(), :has() and pseudo-classes in general only remove or re-target and never add, a base that matches nothing PROVES the original matches nothing; a base that matches leaves the answer true (may match), which reports the rule rather than guessing. So 'h1:hover' and 'h1:not(.x)' are reported and '.checklist li:not(.x)' is skipped, neither throwing.
  - a pseudo-element styles a generated box, never the element itself, so a branch containing '::' is false.
  - '+' and '~' need sibling information the chain does not carry. Decide the rightmost compound first, because that much is provable with no tree ('h1 + p' is false, since the page h1 is not a p); anything that gets past it returns true.
This removes the whitelist that caused BUG-1 and the throw that caused BUG-4. The four assert.throws cases in 'the cascade resolver agrees with CSS on specificity' are re-specified against the new guarantee rather than deleted: a selector that may reach is reported, one that provably cannot is skipped, and both directions are asserted.

The rule the guard now implements, stated once, because AC-11, the tests and the failure message must not disagree about it. A rule is REPORTED when either ground holds: (a) it may match the page h1 AND outranks the page-title class rule on font-size, line-height or a top margin — higher specificity, or equal and later, and !important outranks specificity asymmetrically; or (b) it may match the ROOT element (chain[0]) and declares font-size or the font shorthand. It is SILENT when it provably cannot match the h1, when it does match the h1 but loses the cascade to the class rule, and when it declares none of the three guarded properties — with one exception that is ground (b), not a third rule: '*' appears in the reach list and in the reported list at once, because a font-size on it moves the root, while a non-font declaration on it is silent. The ground (b) test is about the ROOT element, not about the h1: an attribute selector naming an attribute the h1 does not carry ('[data-x="a b"]') is a provable no-match for the h1, but one naming an attribute the root does carry ('[lang]', since the root is <html lang="en">) is a ground-(b) report. Getting those two the wrong way round is what produced the reviewer's objection and the second error in this revision, so it is stated here in the contract and asserted on both sides.

5 — Compare the resolved value, not the winning declaration (BUG-2). Add one exported constant naming the declaration each guarded group must finally be settled by — { 'font-size': 'font-size: 1.4rem', 'line-height': 'line-height: 1.25', 'margin-top': 'margin: 0' } — and have BOTH tests read it: the declaration test asserts the class rule contains each of those, and the cascade test compares the class rule's WINNING declaration for that group against it, ignoring any !important. A stylesheet declaring .page-title twice now reports: the second rule's 2.4rem is what the cascade keeps, so the page h1's font-size would be 2.4rem instead of font-size: 1.4rem. Keep the three existing literal assertions in the declaration test — the values must stay visible in the test, not only in a table.

6 — Ground (b), the root font-size (new, and it is what makes ground (a) honest). For every rule that is not a class rule, if branchReaches(branch, chain, 0) and the branch declares font-size or font, push an offender under the font-size and line-height groups with its own message: the selector changes the root element's font-size, and the class rule's own rem values are measured against it, so the page title's font-size moves even though the class rule wins the cascade on the element. Measured on the shipped tree, each of these renders the h1 at something other than 22.4px: '* { font-size: 2.4rem }' 53.76px, '* { font: 700 2.4rem system-ui }' 53.76px, 'html { font-size: 2.4rem }' 53.76px, 'html, body { font-size: 2.4rem }' 53.76px, 'html { font-size: 20px }' 28px, ':root { font-size: 20px }' 28px, 'html, body { font-size: 20px }' 28px, and '[lang] { font-size: 2.4rem }' 53.76px — the last because the root carries lang. 'body { font-size: 20px }', 'main { font-size: 20px }' and '#main { font-size: 20px }' all render 22.4px and stay silent, because rem is measured against the root and the body is not the root. The shipped stylesheet is unaffected: of its 60 rules, the only root-reaching ones are ':root' (custom properties) and '*' (box-sizing), neither of which declares font-size or font, and the only rule among the 15 that touch a guarded property and can reach the h1 is .page-title itself, so the clean tree stays CLEAN.

7 — Keep what was already right. The !important model (importance outranks specificity, asymmetrically, and an ancestor's !important is still only an inherited value), the winner-selection rule across several class rules, the @media/@supports lifting with the condition named in the message, the shorthand-to-group reporting, the message wording that names the selector and the property, and the three pinning tests for the class extractor, the call site and the class-name exception. Change nothing about how a rule is turned into declarations or how specificity is compared; change only what 'this selector can match the h1' means, and add the one question about the value.

8 — Pin the new guard. Every case above needs a test: the four QA repros verbatim, the root repro, the element-derived chain, the one-directional property in all three directions (provable no-match, reach-and-outrank, reach-but-lose), the ground-(b) report on '[lang]', and the coordinated-rename green. Keep the existing ~25 guard cases. Re-express, do not delete, the four cases that asserted the throw, and re-state the case that currently reads "'*' reaches every element but loses to the class rule at (0,1,0), so the heading is unaffected": that sentence is false in the browser (53.76px, measured), so the case becomes two — '*' declaring font-size is reported under ground (b), and '*' declaring something else on a guarded property stays silent under ground (a). The previous revision's risks[0] said a case that cannot be re-expressed against the new guarantee is a stop rather than something to delete quietly; this one can be, and the reason is ground (b).

(2) Add one quote- and bracket-aware splitCompounds(branch) that tracks bracket/paren depth and quote state and breaks only on whitespace, '>', '+' or '~' outside them, and that does not emit an empty compound for the spaces around a '>' ('main > h1' is two compounds, not three); treat a newline as whitespace, because the shipped sheet has a comma list broken across one. risks: The rewrite replaces a guard that works on the shapes it was written for with one that works on the shapes the markup actually contains. Every case the previous attempt pinned must be re-run against the new matcher, and the ones that assert the throw have to be re-expressed rather than copied. The previous revision said a case that cannot be re-expressed is a stop rather than something to delete quietly; there is now exactly one such case, the '*' case, and it CAN be re-expressed because ground (b) gives it an answer — re-stated, never deleted.

Over-approximating reachability is deliberately the noisy direction, and ground (b) widens it further. A rule that MAY match the page h1 and outranks the class rule is reported, so a future stylesheet using a functional pseudo-class on the h1, or a sibling combinator, turns the build red rather than being skipped. On top of that, ANY rule that may match the root and declares font-size or the font shorthand is now reported: '* { font-size: … }', 'html { font-size: … }', ':root { font-size: … }', and any attribute selector naming an attribute the root carries, '[lang]'. A ':root { font-size: 62.5% }' type-scale reset is ordinary CSS and will now turn the build red until the page title's held value is restated, which is the same contract AC-2 and AC-8 already impose on the class rule's own values. That is a behaviour change from attempt 1, which passed on all of these; it is the right direction (a report is a failure, never a false pass) and it is a real cost, so it is named here rather than discovered.

Ground (b) is the ground most easily misapplied, because it asks about the ROOT while the rest of the guard asks about the h1. Two of this order's revisions got it wrong in opposite directions — the first filed '[lang]' as a provable no-match, the second nearly filed 'h1[data-testid="page title"]' as a report — and both errors are invisible without rendering the case. The contract in approach §4 states the distinction in one sentence for exactly this reason, and AC-11, AC-12 and the tests[] cases now assert both sides. Treat a reclassification of any attribute selector as a change to a guard, not an edit to a list.

The element chain is read from the rendered markup of one route, so the guard reasons about '/' and assumes the other four shells put the h1 in the same place. That is already pinned by AC-6 and by the 25-shell test, and layout() is the only producer of the h1, so the assumption holds today. If a future page ever nests the h1 differently, this guard's world-model is wrong for that page and the failure is a missed report rather than a false alarm.

The specificity arithmetic is unchanged but now shares its splitter with the matcher, so a selector shape that tokenises differently between the two would mis-order the cascade. Keeping both on one splitter is the mitigation, and a case that pins the two against the same selector list is worth adding if the implementer has budget.

This is still a test helper that makes a claim about CSS, which is the same failure mode the ticket was filed for. It is mitigated by the one-directional contract — there is no shape that yields a silent pass, only shapes that yield a false failure — but a change to the guard's vocabulary is a change to a guard and belongs in its own commit with its own pinned cases.

The class-name assertion remains a deliberate exception to .sdlc/memory/qa/selectors.md, which is owned by the Librarian and still does not record it. The new guard leans on the data-testid hook rather than the class, which reduces how much rests on the exception, but the pin itself is still there and the Librarian's note is still owed on #51.
